description:
Climate ventures fail for predictable reasons: unit economics that do not work, pilots that never leave the building, and measurement nobody can defend.

This session follows three real projects from first sketch to field deployment, including the failures. We cover impact measurement, first pilot design, and the funding conversations that actually happen.
summary: What it genuinely takes to move a climate idea out of a notebook and into a pilot that survives contact with reality.
title: CLIMATE TECH: FROM IDEA TO FIELD.

agenda: 05:40 PM — How open source actually works
description:
Contributing to open source looks impossible from the outside and is genuinely approachable from the inside, once someone shows you how a project is put together.

We walk through reading an unfamiliar codebase, finding an issue worth fixing, and making a contribution that a maintainer will actually accept. You will leave with a contribution you have made in the session, a shortlist of projects suited to your interests, and the vocabulary to ask maintainers good questions.
summary: How to go from a GitHub tab you have bookmarked to a merged pull request — without pretending the learning curve does not exist.
title: YOUR FIRST OPEN SOURCE CONTRIBUTION.

description:
A design sprint compresses an entire design cycle into a focused week. In this workshop we run the core of it live: map the challenge, sketch wildly, decide with intent, and prototype something a real person can react to.

You will work in a small group, experience how quickly a team can converge when the process is disciplined, and leave with a method you can apply to your own coursework and projects.
summary: Five days, five days of decisions, one tested idea — the structured process behind the product everyone else is still discussing.
title: THE ART OF THE DESIGN SPRINT.

certificateNote: A certificate of participation is issued to everyone who attends the full session.
description:
The question is no longer whether AI will take your work. It is whether the people using it well will.

This workshop is a practical, non-technical session for students who want to build genuine leverage with AI rather than outsource their judgement to it. We start with what has actually changed in the labour market, then work through the specific tasks where AI helps, where it quietly makes things worse, and where a thoughtful human being is simply irreplaceable.

Expect real examples, a frank conversation about productivity culture, and a set of habits you can take back to your coursework, your projects and your first job.
summary: A working session on using AI as leverage instead of a crutch — what to automate, what to keep, and how to stay the person who does the thinking.
title:
AI ISN'T REPLACING YOU.
A PERSON USING IT MIGHT.

description:
Most speaking advice is about confidence. This is about structure, which is easier.

You will rehearse a two-minute talk three times during the session and get specific, useful feedback each round. We cover opening lines that do not put the audience to sleep, how to recover from losing your place, and how to sound like yourself rather than a presenter.
summary: Structure, nerves and the first thirty seconds — a rehearsal-based session for anyone who has ever rehearsed a talk alone in the shower.
title: PUBLIC SPEAKING FOR THE CAMERA-SHY.

description:
Your first committee is confusing until someone explains the mechanics. This session covers how resolutions are drafted and negotiated, what a decent speech needs to contain, and the motions that decide whether your committee moves forward or stalls.

We finish with a short mock committee so you leave knowing exactly what to do when the gavel comes down.
summary: How a Model UN conference actually runs, and how to be genuinely useful in your first session.
title: MUN 101: YOUR FIRST COMMITTEE.
